title: Covering the Query to Kill the Key Lookup
description: An index that seeks but doesn't carry the returned columns does a Key Lookup per row; INCLUDE them to make the seek covering. Why it matters: key lookups multiply cost per row returned -- at scale, eliminating them is often the single biggest win available on a hot code path.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

This lesson is a close, practical companion to the earlier covering-index lesson, showing the same core idea — an index that seeks but doesn't fully cover a query still leaves behind an expensive Key Lookup — in a slightly different, very common real-world shape: a support dashboard listing all tickets assigned to one agent.

There's already an index on `AssignedTo`, and the query plan does successfully seek into it — so at first glance, this looks like a success story, not a problem. But the plan still does far more reads than you'd expect to return roughly 150 tickets, because the index on `AssignedTo` only contains `AssignedTo` itself (plus the underlying clustered key needed to find the rest of the row) — it doesn't contain `Priority`, or whatever other columns the dashboard's `SELECT` list actually needs to display. So for every one of those ~150 matching tickets, SQL Server has to take a side trip back to the full table (a **Key Lookup** — think of it as the index handing you a pointer that says "the rest of the details for this row are over on page X of the actual table," which the engine then has to go fetch) to retrieve the remaining columns.

It's worth restating the core mental model here because it's genuinely one of the most important ideas in everyday SQL Server performance tuning: an index seek tells you *which rows* match your filter, cheaply and quickly — but it only tells you about the *columns that are actually stored in that index*. If your `SELECT` list asks for anything beyond what the index contains, each matching row needs an additional trip back to the full table to grab the missing pieces. For a small number of matching rows, this is barely noticeable — a handful of extra page reads, nothing that shows up as a real problem. But "a handful of extra reads, repeated once per matching row" is exactly the kind of cost that scales directly with how many rows match, and 150 lookups (one per ticket) is enough to make the query noticeably more expensive than it needs to be, even though the underlying seek itself was fast.

The fix, once again, is to make the index **covering**: add the columns the dashboard actually displays (`Priority`, and whatever else is in the `SELECT` list) as `INCLUDE` columns on the existing index — `CREATE INDEX IX_Tickets_AssignedTo ON Tickets(AssignedTo) INCLUDE (Priority, ...)`. This doesn't change what the index is *searchable by* (it's still keyed only on `AssignedTo`, so it still seeks the same way it always did) — it just means that once the engine finds a matching row via the seek, everything the query needs is already sitting right there in the index entry itself, with no need to go fetch anything else from the underlying table. The plan changes from "Seek, then Key Lookup ×150" to a single clean "Index Seek" that returns everything in one pass.

This lesson is worth treating as a second, reinforcing example of the covering-index concept rather than a brand-new idea, precisely because this exact shape — "there's an index, the plan does seek it, but I still see a Key Lookup sitting next to the seek in the execution plan, and it's doing noticeably more reads than expected" — is genuinely one of the single most common performance patterns you'll encounter in real applications. Support dashboards, order lists, "my assigned items" views, admin panels — basically any screen that filters to one entity (one agent, one customer, one project) and then displays a handful of extra descriptive columns alongside the filtered rows — tends to hit exactly this pattern, because the natural way to design an index (index the column you filter by) doesn't automatically account for what other columns the display also needs.

Why does this matter as a repeatable skill, not just a one-off fix? Because once you learn to recognize the visual signature in an execution plan — a Key Lookup operator connected via a Nested Loops join to an Index Seek — you'll be able to fix this exact class of problem quickly and confidently across an enormous range of real, everyday queries, simply by asking "what columns does my SELECT list need that aren't already part of this index's key or INCLUDE list?" and adding them.

It's worth treating this lesson, alongside the earlier covering-index lesson, as establishing a general checklist you can run through any time you look at a query plan and see a Key Lookup: first, confirm the seek itself is using the right index (the filtering column matches); second, look at what columns the SELECT list, any GROUP BY, and any ORDER BY actually need; third, check whether all of those columns are already part of the index's key or INCLUDE list; and if not, add the missing ones as INCLUDE columns. This three-step check is fast to run, essentially risk-free to apply (INCLUDE columns don't change what the index is searchable by, so you're not at risk of breaking some other query that relies on the same index), and addresses one of the single most common, highest-value performance issues you'll find across ordinary business queries — dashboards, list views, and reports that filter to one thing and then display a handful of extra descriptive fields alongside it.

One more thing worth knowing: it's worth periodically reviewing your most frequently-run dashboard and report queries specifically for this pattern, even ones that already 'work fine,' because a Key Lookup that costs a little today can become a much bigger cost tomorrow as the matching row count grows -- proactively covering your busiest queries is usually cheaper than waiting for a complaint about slowness to prompt the investigation.

As a final practical note, this same checklist applies just as well to queries you're writing for the very first time, not only ones you're troubleshooting after the fact -- when designing a brand-new index to support a brand-new query, it costs nothing extra to think through the full SELECT list up front and include every needed column from the start, rather than discovering the missing columns later once a Key Lookup shows up in a slow query report.

## Scenario
A support dashboard lists all tickets for one agent. There's already an index on `AssignedTo`, and the plan does seek it — yet it still does hundreds of extra reads to return ~150 tickets.

## Why it's slow
`IX_Tickets_AssignedTo` indexes only `AssignedTo`. The query also returns `Priority` and `Subject`, which live in the clustered index. So for **every** row the seek finds, SQL Server runs back to the base table to fetch those columns — a **Key Lookup** (shown as a **Nested Loops** joining the seek to a Clustered Index Seek). One lookup per matching row adds up fast.

## What to look for
- An Index Seek feeding a **Nested Loops** into a Clustered Index Seek (that pair *is* the Key Lookup).
- Logical reads far larger than the handful of pages the matching rows occupy.

## The concept
Make the index **cover** the query: add the extra output columns as `INCLUDE` columns so they're stored in the index leaf. Then the seek returns everything the query needs in one pass — no trip back to the base table, no Nested Loops, a fraction of the reads. INCLUDE columns don't affect the key order; they just ride along to eliminate lookups.
hints: The seek is fine; the cost is the per-row trip back to the clustered index (a Key Lookup, shown as Nested Loops) to get Priority and Subject.
If the index carried Priority and Subject too, no lookup would be needed.
Rebuild the index to cover the query: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Tickets_AssignedTo ON Tickets(AssignedTo) INCLUDE (Priority, Subject) WITH (DROP_EXISTING = ON);
